cells.tense: You are meeting the endings as they come, and you let them settle.
cells.ask: Pick one thing that has already finished and say out loud, once, that it's over. Then leave it alone for the rest of the day.
cells.core:
You're not dragging anything behind you. Things end, you let them end, and you're not standing in front of a closed door arguing with it. That sounds small until you watch somebody spend years at the same closed door.

It isn't passivity either. You say this is over, you mean it, and the same attention goes onto what's next. Finishing and beginning are one motion for you, so neither one costs much. Fairness stays easy too. You hand things back, you let things come, and you don't keep a tally about who owes what. One thing to hold: end something by choice this week, before it wears out on its own. That's the upkeep.
cells.sheetLine: You let things end, and you don't argue with the closed door.
cells.verb: Ending what has finished so what comes next can start.
cells.place: In the room where you point your attention and choose the direction.

cells.tense: You are bracing for the next ending while the current one is still mid-sentence.
cells.ask: Name one thing you were about to end and give it a fixed date to live until. Do nothing about it before that date.
cells.core:
A month in and the exit is already mapped. New job, new person, new city, new plan — and you leave before it can disappoint you, and you call the leaving freedom. Part of it is freedom. Part of it is flinching early at something that hasn't happened yet.

What you clear out isn't finished. It's still alive and unfinished, and you're ending it to avoid being there when it decides what it is. Your endings aren't wrong; they just arrive before there's anything to end. The correction isn't to stop ending things. It's to feel what's actually there and let that tell you when, instead of deciding ahead of the evidence.
cells.sheetLine: You end things early, then call the exit freedom.
cells.verb: Ending what has finished so what comes next can start.
cells.place: In the room where you point your attention and choose the direction.

cells.tense: You are holding something finished with both hands, and calling the grip loyalty.
cells.ask: Open the drawer or folder that holds it, set ten minutes on a timer, and touch one thing in there.
cells.core:
There's something you're carrying because putting it down looks like an insult to the years it took. You won't say it's finished, so saying it out loud stays out of reach. The job, the city, the version of you that did it — it stays alive on purpose, because closing it out looks like a verdict on the whole thing.

But holding something that's finished isn't loyalty. It's a way of not having to decide anything. You're good at not deciding right now, and the price is quiet: nothing new gets a turn while the finished thing holds the whole room. The ability to end it is sitting right there. What hasn't shown up yet is the appetite to.
cells.sheetLine: You're loyal to something that finished, and the grip is the cost.
cells.verb: Ending what has finished so what comes next can start.
cells.place: In the room where you point your attention and choose the direction.

cells.tense: Something has already ended, and you are still describing it in the present tense.
cells.ask: Write one line: a thing you've stopped doing in the last year without deciding to. Nothing else.
cells.core:
You've been steering this and calling it just how things go. Look at what you've quietly stopped doing — stopped calling someone, stopped showing up somewhere, stopped using a word you used to use. That isn't drift. That's you, ending things, without a meeting about it.

And it works. Your days keep a shape; things line up around you without much noise. That's a real thing you do for people. What's not there is the saying-so. You're surprised when someone mentions the change, and then you agree, because they're right. Next time you say something is over out loud, look at the sentence before you hand it away. It came from you.
cells.sheetLine: You're already ending things and calling it how things go.
cells.verb: Ending what has finished so what comes next can start.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim is that the person is currently in a transformation at all; the reader might say nothing is ending, this is just a stretch of ordinary life, which is exactly the Too Little and Unacknowledged ground, so the ask survives it. The sentence that serves the writer more than the person would be any line that promises renewal or names what is dying; I have kept both out. The asks are doable today with no money, no audience, no free time beyond a minute, and none of them makes progress depend on obeying.
